units.title: Stablecoin-native L1s
angles: Transaction types. For every transaction type and execution context this network adds (batches, sponsored or fee-token transactions, deposits, retryables, system calls, account abstraction, delegated accounts), work out what msg.sender, msg.value and transient storage look like inside the PoolManager and walk unlock, sync, settle and take through each.

Sweep. List every precompile, predeploy, system contract, face of the native asset, wrapped native token, bridge, staking and fee contract on this network. For each one, run eth_call with "from" set to the PoolManager address for the call shapes P1, P2, P3 and P5 in ASSUMPTIONS.md (empty calldata with zero value, transfer(address,uint256) with zero and nonzero amount, balanceOf(PoolManager), and each IHooks selector), and record what comes back. Follow up on every target that does not revert.

units.title: HyperEVM
angles: Exits. Can an ordinary account make another user's swap or liquidity removal impossible to include or always revert on this network (gas caps, storage pricing, per-transaction limits, tick crossing cost, special recipients)?

Known weaknesses. Collect security advisories, audit reports, bug bounty write-ups, incident post-mortems and open issues for this network's execution client, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years, including behaviour the network calls by design. For each, decide whether an ordinary account could use it against funds in the PoolManager.

units.title: High-throughput chains with modified gas models
angles: Faces. Find every way one balance at the PoolManager can be reached under two currency ids or in two units on this network (native asset with an ERC-20 face, wrapped native predeploys, bridged and canonical versions sharing storage, tokens with more than one entry point), and walk sync, settle, take, mint and burn across the two faces in every order.

Pooled assets. Read the PoolManager's largest token balances on this network from chain. For each token, check transfer and balanceOf for behaviour any holder can trigger: rebasing, fees, callbacks, share accounting, special recipients, special amounts.

code.task: Answers lead L-257; report it in leadResults. Goal: on each of the 21 networks, list every pooled token whose balance at the PoolManager moves without a Transfer log that names the PoolManager, or whose Transfer logs move a different amount than the balance. Method: take the currencies from the Initialize logs of the PoolManager (currency0 and currency1 are indexed topics) over as long a range as the endpoint serves, or from the explorer's token holdings page of the PoolManager address where logs are not served, and keep those with a balance above dust. For each, pick two blocks B1 and B2 at least a day apart where the endpoint serves old state (otherwise the widest window it serves), read balanceOf(PoolManager) at both, sum the Transfer logs to and from the PoolManager in between, and compare. Work in bulk with python3 and batch JSON-RPC, and keep the scripts and raw results in your output directory. For every token that does not reconcile, read its source or trace it and classify: rebase up, rebase down, reward push, fee on transfer, share rate, balance that depends on a price or on another contract, clawback or burn by a role, block list. Then answer for each: can an ordinary account choose the moment or the size of the change (a public rebase, poke, harvest, claim-for, checkpoint or price update function), can it raise the PoolManager's reported balance inside one transaction and have it fall back later, and what does sync then settle, or take then repay, yield at today's pooled amount (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289 and 349-365). A balance that an ordinary account can raise between sync and settle and that later falls back takes other users' funds and is a high finding; say plainly when the surplus was never anyone's. Also list tokens where the reported balance can fall below what pools are owed, because the last users to withdraw are then locked. Do not repeat what F-012, F-037, F-041 and F-060 already cover (stETH, aTokens, AMPL, qiAVAX); name new tokens and new networks.

Answers lead L-259; report it in leadResults. take lets any account, inside its own unlock, make the PoolManager send its whole balance of a token and receive it back before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 349-365, src/types/Currency.sol:40-80). The PoolManager is one address for all pools on a network. Find every pooled token and every network rule under which that round trip, repeated at no cost but gas, leaves the PoolManager address in a worse state for the next user. Look for: a cap on the volume or number of transfers one address may send or receive per block, per day or per epoch; a cooldown between transfers; a maximum balance per holder; velocity or anomaly rules of an issuer or of a compliance precompile that flag or freeze an address automatically; rate limited bridged tokens (xERC20 limits, CCTP or OFT rate limits, Superchain token bridge limits) whose transfer path checks a limit; tokens that charge or burn per transfer from the holder's remaining balance; tokens that record the last transfer block of an address and reject a second movement in the same block; network level rules that throttle or deprioritise an account by the state or gas it has used (MegaETH per-account or per-block resource budgets, Monad reserve balance rules, HyperEVM block type selection, Tempo and Arc policy registries, BNB and Polygon system rules, sequencer side filters on the OP Stack and Nitro chains). Take token lists from the earlier cycle files in research/network-risk/cycles/ and from explorers, and include the stock tokens and USDG on Robinhood Chain, the Securitize wrappers and multiplier tokens on X Layer, wrapped stock tokens on Monad and Ink, SPCXB, B20 tokens on Base, TIP-20 tokens under TIP-403 policies on Tempo, wBRL and wARS on Celo. For each rule found, read the token or client source, state whether an ordinary account can trip it for the PoolManager address without holding the token (the take is repaid in the same unlock, so no capital is needed beyond gas), how long other users' takes and settles then fail, and what it costs. Test with read-only calls where a view exposes the remaining allowance of an address. A rule that an ordinary account can trip to block other users' withdrawals is an in-scope freeze.

The unlock flag, the deltas, the nonzero delta count and the synced currency with its reserves all live in transient storage, which lasts for one transaction and is shared by everything that runs in it (src/libraries/Lock.sol, CurrencyDelta.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol, CurrencyReserves.sol). sync needs no lock and leaves the synced currency and reserves set when the call ends (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289). So whenever one transaction carries calls from several unrelated users, an earlier user can leave transient state that a later user's call meets. First, for each of the 21 networks list every way that calls of different users end up in one transaction: ERC-4337 bundles through each deployed EntryPoint version (handleOps runs all operations in one transaction), EIP-7702 batch executors and relayers, Tempo type 0x76 batches with a fee payer and Tempo sponsored transactions, World Chain priority bundles, Arc CallFrom and its helper contracts, intent settlement contracts and solver batches (UniswapX reactors, CoW settlement, 1inch Fusion, Across, Bebop), sequencer or builder level bundle transactions, HyperEVM system transactions, Celo and X Layer fee abstraction, and multicall style public relayers. Establish from source or a trace that they share one transient map. Second, write down every state an ordinary user can leave behind for the next user in the same transaction: synced currency X with reserves R, where R may be lower or higher than the balance at the time the victim acts (the attacker can move tokens to or from the PoolManager after sync by a plain transfer, or by take and settle inside an unlock that has ended). Note that deltas and the lock are always zero when unlock returns. Third, read how the routers that ordinary users rely on pay the PoolManager, from their verified source on the explorers: the Universal Router and v4 PositionManager at the addresses in state/networks.json or the deployments page, and the two or three most used third party routers per network. For each: does it always call sync before a token settle, does it call sync(address(0)) or rely on the slot being zero before a native settle with value, does it ever call settle without a sync of its own, does it read exttload of the reserves slots, does it use settleFor. Then decide for each leftover state and each router: does the victim's call revert (a denial that the attacker can repeat in every bundle), or is the victim's payment credited to the wrong currency, credited short, or credited to someone else. In particular walk this order: attacker syncs token X while the PoolManager holds R, then sends some X to the PoolManager by plain transfer or removes some through an earlier unlock; the victim's router then pays X or pays native. Who is credited what (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365)? Also check whether a victim who pays a token leaves a surplus that the attacker, running later in the same transaction, can settle to itself. Report a wrong credit or a capture as a finding with the bundle type and router named; report a repeatable denial with its cost.
